0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
Of all the churches Paul founded, none gave him more grief — or more glory — than the church at Corinth. Corinth was one of the great cities of the ancient world: a rebuilt Roman colony on the narrow isthmus of Greece, sitting athwart the trade routes of the Mediterranean, a cosmopolitan, polyglot, ferociously commercial city where every culture, every religion, and every vice was for sale. The Greek verb korinthiazesthai — to live like a Corinthian — had become a byword for sexual immorality. Into this city Paul came on his second missionary journey around AD 50, stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11), and planted a church that would make him simultaneously the most celebrated and most embattled apostle in his own lifetime.

He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 54–55, provoked by reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. What he had heard was alarming: the church had fractured into personality factions (“I follow Paul”; “I follow Apollos”; “I follow Cephas”; “I follow Christ”); a man was openly sleeping with his stepmother and the church was proud of its tolerance; members were suing each other in pagan courts; spiritual gifts had become instruments of status and one-upmanship; the Lord’s Supper had been turned into a class exercise in social humiliation; and some were denying the bodily resurrection entirely. This is a church in crisis — not the crisis of persecution from outside, but the far more dangerous crisis of pride, worldliness, and theological confusion from within.

Paul’s answer to every single one of these crises is the same: the cross. The word of the cross (1:18) is the only wisdom that addresses human arrogance. The crucified Christ (1:23) is the only foundation (3:11) on which a community can be built. The resurrection of Christ (15:20) is the only ground on which the resurrection of the dead makes sense. Every pastoral problem in the letter — from church discipline to spiritual gifts to the collection for the Jerusalem poor — is resolved by returning to the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. This is why Martin Luther said that the theology of the cross (theologia crucis) stands against the theology of glory (theologia gloriae) at every point, and why this letter is the most searching diagnostic of the church’s recurrent temptation to dress the gospel in the clothing of worldly wisdom and power.

The commentary that follows draws on Gordon Fee’s magnificent NICNT volume, Anthony Thiselton’s exhaustive NIGTC commentary, Roy Ciampa and Brian Rosner’s Pillar NT Commentary, Calvin’s Commentary on 1 Corinthians, Thomas Schreiner, John MacArthur, and the preaching of Timothy Keller on the Corinthian epistles. The governing conviction is that this letter was written to the twenty-first century as much as the first — because the Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world simultaneously.

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Romans opens with a theological masterwork; 1 Corinthians opens with a pastoral emergency. By verse 10, Paul is already addressing the fractures tearing the Corinthian community apart. But before the rebuke comes the gospel — and in the greeting and thanksgiving of the opening nine verses, Paul quietly plants every seed he will spend sixteen chapters watering. The Corinthians are sanctified, called, enriched in speech and knowledge, not lacking in any spiritual gift, and sustained by a faithful God. They are spiritually wealthy — which is precisely what makes their quarrelling so tragic.

The great movement of the chapter is from human division (vv. 10–17) to divine wisdom (vv. 18–31). The factional loyalties at Corinth are not merely a personality problem; they are a theological problem, because they reveal that the Corinthians have been seduced by the world’s categories of wisdom, power, and prestige. Paul’s counter-move is devastating in its simplicity: the cross. The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God (v. 18). God has chosen what is foolish, weak, and despised — and thereby destroyed every human ground of boasting. The chapter ends where the entire letter must end: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s greeting is terse by ancient standards — a mere three verses — but every word is doing theological work. He identifies himself as an apostle by the will of God, not by human appointment or apostolic succession. The commission he carries belongs to Christ; it was given, not chosen. Sosthenes, named as co-sender, is almost certainly the former synagogue ruler of Corinth (Acts 18:17), now a brother in Christ — a walking testimony to the power of the gospel to transform its opponents.

The address to the Corinthians is the most remarkable thing in the greeting: they are “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints.” Sanctified — present tense, passive voice. Their holiness is not an achievement but a location: they are holy because they are in Christ, who is holy. This matters enormously for a letter that will spend much of its time rebuking their decidedly unholy behaviour: Paul never stops addressing them as saints. He rebukes them as people who already are what he is calling them to become. The gospel pronounces identity before it issues imperatives.

The universal address — “together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” — opens the letter to the whole church catholic. This is not merely a letter to Corinth; it is a letter for every community that calls on the name of Christ. Grace and peace — the charter of the redeemed life — come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, placed on the same level of divine gift-giving with a naturalness that is one of Paul’s most powerful incidental arguments for the deity of the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul’s self-designation as an apostle “by the will of God” is not modesty but theology. The divine will is the only ground of any apostolic or ministerial commission. This will become crucial in the letter: when the Corinthians reject Paul’s apostleship, they are not rejecting a self-appointed teacher but the will of the God who sent him. The same logic applies to their own calling: they are saints not because they volunteered but because they were called (v. 2). The sovereignty of grace is the foundation of every sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s apostolic authority was contested at Corinth by those who preferred Apollos’s rhetorical polish or Cephas’s Petrine prestige. His opening — “called by the will of God” — quietly answers the challenge before it is raised. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still the same: divine calling, not human talent. The pastor who grounds his authority in his own gifts is standing on sand; the one who grounds it in the call of God can stand when the culture turns against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary: Three words carry the theological weight: klētos (called), thelēmatos theou (will of God), apostolos (apostle). Paul does not say “Paul, who became an apostle” or “Paul, who was trained as an apostle” — he was called to it, by a divine will that preceded his own. The Damascus road was not an application Paul submitted; it was an arrest God made. Sosthenes’s presence here is quietly significant: the former synagogue ruler who had Paul beaten before the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:12–17) now writes alongside him. The gospel conquers its adversaries.

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The church of God that is in Corinth” — a community defined by its divine ownership before its geographic location. “Sanctified in Christ Jesus” is a completed past action (perfect passive participle): their consecration was accomplished at the moment of their union with Christ. “Called to be saints” is not an invitation to moral striving but a statement of status. The universality of “in every place call upon the name of our Lord” anchors Corinth in the one worldwide fellowship of those who invoke Christ as Lord — a title that in the LXX is the name of God. The yoking of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ as the joint source of grace and peace is, characteristically for Paul, a trinitarian statement disguised as a salutation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul almost always begins his letters with a thanksgiving, and the thanksgivings are never mere formality — they are theological previews of the letter’s concerns. Here the irony runs deep: he thanks God for the Corinthians’ richness in speech and knowledge, for their possession of every spiritual gift — the very things that have become sources of pride and division. Paul is not being sarcastic; he is being theological. The gifts are real. The enrichment is genuine. The problem is not that they have these gifts but that they have mistaken the gifts for the Giver, and begun to boast in their spiritual portfolio rather than in the One who gave it.

The theological pivot of the thanksgiving is v. 7: “as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Every spiritual gift is a provisional equipment for the period between the first and second coming. The gifts are not ends in themselves; they are tools for waiting and working. And underneath all of them is the foundation that cannot shift: “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord” (v. 9). The Corinthians’ security does not rest on their gifts, their eloquence, their knowledge, or their loyalty to the right apostle. It rests on the faithfulness of the God who called them.

This is the note Paul sounds before he says a single word of rebuke — and it is the most pastoral move in the letter. He does not open with accusation but with affirmation of what God has done. The gospel is gift before it is demand; identity before it is imperative.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 — “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” — is one of the great perseverance texts in Paul. The guarantee of the Corinthians’ ultimate confirmation (v. 8) is not their grip on Christ but God’s grip on them. The calling is God’s act; the fellowship is God’s gift; the sustaining is God’s work. Reformed theology has always grounded the doctrine of perseverance here: the saints persevere not because they are strong but because the God who called them is faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing before God and their superiority over others by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge. Paul’s thanksgiving subtly reorients them: the gifts are something you “were enriched in” — given, not earned. Now: The same pride attaches to spiritual accomplishment in every generation — the sense that one’s theological sophistication or spiritual experience gives one a higher standing. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. What do you have that you did not receive? (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary: The thanksgiving is entirely God-directed: Paul thanks God for the grace given in Christ — a perfect passive indicating a completed transaction. The Corinthians did not generate their gifts; they received them. “Enriched” (eploutisthēte) is the same word Paul will use in 2 Corinthians 8:9: though Christ was rich, he became poor, so that they through his poverty might become rich. Their wealth is Christ’s poverty — his death — applied to them. “All speech and all knowledge” anticipates the letter’s two great trouble areas: the gift of tongues (ch. 14) and the pride of knowledge (ch. 8). Both are real gifts; both have been distorted.

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary: The spiritual gifts are the confirmation of the apostolic testimony — the divine signature on Paul’s preaching. “Not lacking in any gift” is a remarkable statement about a church so evidently lacking in love, humility, and self-control. Yet Paul does not deny the gifts; he recontextualises them. They are equipment for waiting: “as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The gifts are eschatological provision, tools for the interim between the ascension and the Parousia. They are not permanent trophies but temporary provisions — and this will matter enormously when Paul discusses their cessation in chapter 13.

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sustaining is God’s act, not theirs. The word translated “guiltless” (anenklētous) is a legal term: acquitted, with no charge standing against you. On the day of the Lord, the Corinthians — fractious, immoral, arrogant as they are — will stand before the Judge without a charge, because Christ has borne every charge. This is not presumption; it is the logic of the gospel. And the ground of confidence is God’s own character: pistos ho theos — “God is faithful.” He called them into fellowship with his Son; he will keep them in it. Keller: “The most dangerous thing in the world is not a God who might abandon you. It is a God of infinite faithfulness who has committed himself to you.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transition from thanksgiving to rebuke is abrupt and deliberate. Paul does not ease into the problem; he names it: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you.” The word for “divisions” is schismata — tears, splits in fabric. The church at Corinth is tearing apart along lines of apostolic loyalty: some claiming Paul, some Apollos, some Cephas, some Christ. The factions map onto real social and theological differences — Paul’s simplicity of proclamation vs. Apollos’s Alexandrian rhetorical polish vs. the Petrine prestige of Jerusalem connection — and they reveal a church that has imported the ancient world’s habit of social competition into the body of Christ.

Paul’s response is not to defend himself but to redirect attention to Christ. “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptised in the name of Paul?” The questions are rhetorical but lethal: the only person around whom a Christian community can legitimately cohere is the one who was crucified for them. Paul is actually glad he baptised so few of them — because baptism into his name would have been the precise idolatry the factions are committing. The logic of baptism is that it names the one to whom you belong; to be baptised in Christ’s name is to belong to Christ, not to any apostle.

The climax of the section is v. 17: “For Christ did not send me to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.” This is the hinge of the entire letter’s first section. The cross is the thing that is at stake. Dress it in human rhetorical eloquence and you have improved the packaging while destroying the contents. The power of the gospel is not the power of skillful persuasion; it is the power of God operating through the proclamation of a crucified Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions are a cautionary tale about what happens when human personality becomes the centre of Christian community. Calvin saw in this text a permanent warning: the church that rallies around a preacher’s gifts, style, or personality rather than around the crucified Christ has already drifted from the gospel. The preacher is, at most, a herald — the one who announces a message that does not belong to him. Paul’s refusal to preach with “eloquent wisdom” is not anti-intellectualism; it is a deliberate choice to let the gospel speak in its own register, with its own power, rather than dressing it in borrowed clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and sophistry: you attached yourself to the most impressive teacher, displayed his influence on your life, and measured your social standing by his. The Corinthian factions are simply the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity pastor culture is the contemporary version. The church that streams a famous preacher rather than investing in local pastors, or that divides over which theological tradition’s champion to follow, is still choosing Apollos over Christ — a more impressive package over the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul appeals not by his apostolic authority but by the name of Christ — a name that belongs to all of them equally. The unity he calls for is not uniformity of opinion on every question but “the same mind and the same judgment” — a shared orientation toward Christ that makes factional divisions impossible. The source of Paul’s information is noteworthy: Chloe’s people — household servants or freedpersons, socially marginal figures. Paul has no qualms about receiving reports from the church’s lower social strata, and no pretence that he has not heard what everyone knows.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ or ‘I follow Apollos,’ or ‘I follow Cephas,’ or ‘I follow Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary: Three questions, each more devastating than the last. Is Christ divided? — No: the whole Christ belongs to every believer. Was Paul crucified? — No: the only atoning death in human history was Christ’s. Were you baptised in Paul’s name? — No: baptism is into the name of the One who owns you. The factional boasts are exposed as theologically incoherent: the thing the Corinthians are divided over (apostolic loyalty) is precisely not the thing that can unite them (the crucified Lord). Even the “I follow Christ” faction is rebuked — their super-spiritual claim to Christ alone, bypassing all apostolic mediation, is its own form of pride.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul’s parenthetical correction — “I did baptize also the household of Stephanas” — is humanly charming: the apostle caught in a memory lapse, correcting himself mid-sentence. But the theological point is clear: baptism creates allegiance to Christ, not to the baptiser. Crispus was the synagogue ruler who believed (Acts 18:8); Gaius hosted the whole church (Rom 16:23); Stephanas was the first convert in Achaia (1 Cor 16:15). Paul is grateful that his baptising was limited, because the fewer people can claim a personal bond with him through baptism, the fewer people can build a personality cult on it.

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Emptied of its power” — kenōthē — the verbal form of the noun Paul uses in Philippians 2:7 for the self-emptying of the Son. The cross, if preached with eloquent human wisdom, undergoes a kind of reverse kenosis: what should be the power of God becomes instead a display of the preacher’s skill. The message is neutralised by the medium. This is not false modesty about rhetoric; Paul was an educated man who could write brilliantly. It is a theological commitment: the cross must be allowed to be offensive, foolish, and weak by human standards, so that when it saves, the power is visibly God’s and not the preacher’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Christ the Wisdom and Power of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
These eight verses are among the most concentrated theology in the Pauline corpus. Paul is not simply making a point about preaching style; he is describing a fundamental epistemological rupture between the wisdom of this age and the wisdom of God. The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing — not because it lacks logical coherence but because the natural mind, operating by the world’s categories of power, achievement, and status, cannot process a God who saves by dying. A crucified Messiah is a contradiction in terms by every available measure. The Jews expected a Messiah who would triumph over Rome; they got one who was executed by it. The Greeks prized a wisdom that could be displayed and admired; they got a God who became a spectacle of failure. The cross violated both expectations utterly.

But Paul does not simply defend the cross against these critiques; he turns the categories upside down. The “foolishness” of the cross is wiser than human wisdom; the “weakness” of the cross is stronger than human strength. This is not a paradox that resolves into something more respectable; it is a permanent inversion. God has chosen what the world counts as foolish, weak, and despised — and by that choice, destroyed every human platform of boasting. The cross is not an embarrassment to be apologised for; it is the lens through which the character of God is most fully revealed.

The citation from Isaiah 29:14 — “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise” — places the cross in the long history of God’s pattern of confounding human self-sufficiency. When Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, the wise men of Israel were helpless; God acted alone. When Babylon swept away the temple, the philosophers of the nations had no answer; God restored by promise, not strategy. The cross is the ultimate expression of this pattern: God saves not by leveraging human wisdom but by overturning it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of the Cross (Theologia Crucis)

Luther’s distinction between the theology of the cross and the theology of glory is nowhere more clearly grounded than in 1:18–25. The theologian of glory sees God in power, success, and wisdom that makes sense on human terms. The theologian of the cross sees God revealed precisely in weakness, foolishness, and the apparent defeat of Good Friday. The cross is not the means to something better; it is the place where God is most fully known. Sproul: “The cross is not Plan B after the fall. The cross is Plan A from eternity — the place where the justice and the love of God were both satisfied at the same moment, in the same event, in the same Person.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul wrote into a culture where crucifixion was the ultimate symbol of shame, defeat, and criminal status. To preach a crucified Messiah was not merely theologically offensive but socially disqualifying. The early Christians were not brave about something trivial; they were staking their social standing and their lives on an executed criminal. Now: The pressure to make the gospel more palatable — to lead with Jesus-as-life-coach rather than Jesus-as-sin-bearer, to emphasise personal fulfilment rather than atonement — is the contemporary version of Paul’s Corinthian problem. The cross still offends the wisdom of the age. The answer is still to preach it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
verseByVerse.commentary: “The word of the cross” — not the event of the cross in itself, but the proclaimed word about it. The proclamation is where the power resides. And that power is selective: it is the power of God to those who are being saved (present participle — an ongoing process), foolishness to those who are perishing (also present participle — not yet completed). The citation from Isaiah 29:14 grounds this in OT history: God has always confounded the calculations of the wise when he acts in salvation. The Assyrian crisis, the Babylonian exile, the return from captivity — in every case, human wisdom said it couldn’t be done; God did it anyway. The cross is the supreme instance of this pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul’s rhetorical questions echo Isaiah 19:12 and 33:18 — taunts against the wise counsellors whose wisdom proved useless. The sage, the scribe, the debater represent the three great intellectual traditions: Greek philosophy, Jewish biblical scholarship, and Hellenistic sophistry. All three have been made foolish — not by Paul’s arguments but by God’s action. The logic of v. 21 is profound: it was in God’s wisdom that the world could not know God through wisdom. The very avenue the world was relying on — human reasoning toward the divine — was never able to reach the destination. God must be known by revelation, and the revelation chosen was the “folly” of apostolic preaching about a crucified Saviour.

verseByVerse.quote: For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Signs and wisdom: these are the two currencies of religious credibility in Paul’s world. The Jews expected a Messiah who would authenticate himself by miraculous signs — a military deliverer, a wonder-worker, a visible demonstration of divine power. The Greeks expected wisdom — a coherent, elegant account of reality that could hold its own in the philosophical marketplace. The cross delivers neither on these terms. A Messiah who dies under Roman execution is a stumbling block to every Jewish messianic expectation; a God who reveals himself in apparent defeat is folly to every Greek philosophical aspiration. But to those who are called — and the calling is the key — the same crucified Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. The categories are inverted, not destroyed.

verseByVerse.quote: For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.
verseByVerse.commentary: The statement is deliberately provocative: Paul speaks of the “foolishness” and “weakness” of God — knowing that God has neither, but entering into the world’s perspective to demolish it from within. What appears to be divine foolishness (choosing a crucified Messiah as the means of cosmic redemption) surpasses in wisdom everything human rationality can construct. What appears to be divine weakness (the Son of God dying in agony on a Roman cross) exceeds in power every force the universe can muster. Begg: “When God looks weak, he is about to do something the universe has never seen. Good Friday looked like the defeat of everything. Easter Sunday answered the question.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now invites the Corinthians to look at themselves — and what they see should settle the theological argument definitively. They are not, for the most part, the wise, the powerful, or the well-born. Their own composition as a community is a demonstration of the thesis Paul has been arguing. God chose what is foolish, weak, low, and despised — not because these things have inherent virtue, but in order to nullify the things that do: the wise, the powerful, the strong. The method of grace is subtraction: God takes out of the equation everything that humanity might use as a basis for self-congratulation, so that the only remaining boast is in him.

The citation from Jeremiah 9:24 — “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” — is not an afterthought; it is the goal the whole chapter has been moving toward. The factional boasting of vv. 10–17, the intellectual boasting of vv. 18–25, and the social boasting implicit in the Corinthian culture — all of it is dismantled by the cross and replaced with a single, adequate boast: the Lord who became for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. Everything we need is in him; therefore all boasting must be about him.

Verse 30 is one of Paul’s most concentrated summary statements of the gospel. Christ Jesus “became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption.” Four nouns for what Christ is to the believer. Wisdom: in him we know God truly. Righteousness: in him we stand before God acquitted. Sanctification: in him we are set apart and progressively transformed. Redemption: in him we are bought out of every bondage. The Corinthians were seeking wisdom from Apollos and status from their gifts; Paul says they already have everything in Christ. Their problem is not poverty but ingratitude and forgetfulness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Doctrine of Boasting: Sola Gratia Applied

The logic of vv. 28–29 is the logic of grace pushed to its social conclusion: God chooses the things that are “not” to bring to nothing the things that “are” — “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” This is the pastoral and sociological outworking of sola gratia. If salvation were partly dependent on human wisdom, power, or birth, then at least some people could boast. But when God saves fishermen, tax collectors, former persecutors, and the socially marginal, the only conceivable boast is in the grace that did what human merit could never have achieved. Calvin: “God’s choosing the base things is not an arbitrary preference for lowliness, but a deliberate demolition of all grounds of human pride before him.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth’s social hierarchy was steep and rigid: Roman citizens over freedpersons over slaves; the educated over the illiterate; patrons over clients. The church at Corinth crossed every one of these lines — and the crossing was theological, not merely sociological. It was evidence of the same gospel that the cross proclaimed. Now: The church that unconsciously mirrors the class and status structures of its surrounding culture is denying with its sociology what it affirms with its theology. The cross creates a community where the only legitimate boast is in the Lord — which means no other boast is legitimate at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;
verseByVerse.commentary: “Consider your calling” — the imperative is to look in the mirror. “Not many” — not “none”: there were some wise, powerful, and well-born believers (Crispus, Erastus, Gaius). But they were the exceptions that proved the rule. The pattern of divine election at Corinth is the same pattern as at Bethlehem: God does not choose according to the world’s criteria of impressiveness. The purpose is active: God chose the foolish to shame the wise — not merely to ignore wisdom but to expose its pretensions by surpassing it through foolishness. The shaming is eschatological: at the final judgment, the wisdom that dismissed the cross will stand ashamed before the crucified Lord it despised.

verseByVerse.quote: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Things that are not” — the socially non-existent, the people who do not register in the world’s ledgers of significance. God uses the nothings to nullify the somethings — a reversal so radical it can only be explained by grace. The telos is explicit: “so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.” The method of redemption is designed to close off every avenue of self-congratulation. If God saves through strength, the strong may boast in their strength. If he saves through wisdom, the wise may boast in their wisdom. But when he saves through crucified foolishness, working through the nobodies, there is nothing left to boast in but him.

verseByVerse.quote: And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary: “Because of him you are in Christ Jesus” — the union with Christ is God’s act, not theirs. And in that union, Christ himself became four things for us. Wisdom: not merely a model of wise living but the very wisdom of God made accessible. Righteousness: not merely moral example but imputed right standing before God. Sanctification: not merely moral improvement but actual consecration and ongoing transformation. Redemption: the final deliverance from sin, death, and judgment. These four cover the whole gospel — past justification, present sanctification, future glorification — all located in the person of Christ. The Corinthians were shopping for wisdom from philosophers; it was already theirs in Christ. The Jeremiah citation closes the argument: the only boast that does not collapse under the weight of its own pretension is the boast in the One who gave everything.

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Paul’s extended reflection on why he preached the way he preached when he came to Corinth — and on what kind of wisdom the Spirit actually brings. He came, he says, “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (v. 3). This is not a confession of inadequacy but a theological posture: the deliberate refusal to trust in rhetorical performance, so that the faith of his converts would rest not on human eloquence but on the power of God. The cross, preached without ornament, must do its own work.

The second half of the chapter then opens into one of Paul’s most majestic passages on the Spirit’s role in revelation. There is a wisdom, Paul insists, that is not the wisdom of this age — a hidden wisdom, decreed before the ages, that the rulers of this age did not understand (for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory). This wisdom is revealed by the Spirit alone, because only the Spirit searches the depths of God. The natural person, operating without the Spirit, cannot receive it; the spiritual person, indwelt by the Spirit of God, has the mind of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s self-description in the opening verses of chapter 2 is one of the most important passages in the New Testament on the nature and method of gospel ministry. He came to Corinth without superiority of speech or wisdom. He decided — a deliberate, wilful choice — to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified. He stood before them weak, fearful, trembling. His speech and message were not in plausible words of wisdom.

Why? Not because Paul was incapable of eloquence — his letters prove otherwise — but because the medium must not overwhelm the message. If the Corinthians had been converted by the brilliance of Paul’s rhetoric, their faith would rest on human skill. It would last as long as Paul’s reputation and no longer. But Paul wanted a faith that rested on something sturdier: “the power of God” (v. 5). So he stripped away everything that could have been mistaken for the source of power, and let the cross speak in its own register, authenticated by the Spirit.

The “demonstration of the Spirit and of power” in v. 4 refers not primarily to miracles but to the convicting, converting work of the Holy Spirit through apostolic preaching. When a person hears the message of the cross and believes, something has happened that no human rhetoric could have produced. That is the only demonstration Paul wanted — because it is the only demonstration that cannot be attributed to anything other than God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s deliberate simplicity in proclamation is not a pastoral strategy; it is a doctrinal commitment. The power of the gospel is the power of the Spirit working through the word of the cross — not the power of the preacher, the brilliance of the argument, or the emotional manipulation of the audience. Reformed theology has always insisted on this: it is the Spirit who regenerates, convicts, and converts; the preacher is the instrument, not the cause. Spurgeon: “If men are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything I can add.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth, the travelling sophist was a celebrity figure — a rhetorical virtuoso who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee, and move on. The Corinthians expected their teacher to perform at that level. Paul’s refusal to do so was not incompetence but protest: he would not compete on the sophists’ terms. Now: The contemporary equivalent is the pressure to make church services “compelling” through production values, platform charisma, and emotional manipulation. Paul’s counter-word is not to be deliberately boring, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: actually save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary: “I decided” — ekrina, a deliberate resolution, a settled judgement. Paul did not stumble into simplicity of proclamation; he chose it. “Jesus Christ and him crucified” — specifically the crucifixion, not merely the incarnation or the teaching or the resurrection. The cross is the sharp point of the gospel that cuts through everything. Note that Paul is writing to a church he has already founded and evangelised: “when I came to you” is past tense. He is defending his original method against those who now, having heard Apollos, think they would have preferred something more sophisticated.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Weakness, fear, and much trembling” — this is the apostle Paul describing his own ministry posture. Not weakness from incompetence but weakness as a chosen transparency: the preacher who removes himself from the frame so that Christ fills the canvas. The “demonstration of the Spirit and power” is the Spirit’s own witness to the preached word, producing genuine conviction and conversion that no rhetorical skill could manufacture. And the purpose statement is decisive: their faith must not rest on human wisdom. A faith built on Paul’s eloquence would last until Paul’s reputation faded; a faith built on the power of God is as durable as God himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established what he did not bring — worldly wisdom — Paul now describes what he does bring among the mature: a wisdom that is not of this age. This passage is one of the most profound in the New Testament on the epistemology of faith: how we come to know the things of God. Paul’s answer is startling in its radicalism. The wisdom of God is hidden, secret, decreed before the ages — and utterly inaccessible to the natural human mind. It cannot be reached by philosophical inquiry, mystical ascent, or religious achievement. It can only be revealed — and the revealer is the Spirit of God alone.

The argument moves in a careful analogy. Just as no one knows the thoughts of a person except the spirit of that person, so no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God (v. 11). God’s interior life is opaque to every created mind. But the Spirit has been given to those who believe — which means they have, not a general human spirit that reasons toward God, but the Spirit of God himself, enabling them to know what God has freely given them in Christ. This is the epistemological revolution of the gospel: the believer does not arrive at knowledge of God by ascending; God descends and gives himself to be known.

The “rulers of this age” who crucified the Lord of glory (v. 8) are either the Roman and Jewish authorities involved in the crucifixion, or the demonic powers working behind them, or (most likely) both. Their failure to recognise the Lord of glory in the person of Jesus of Nazareth is not merely a moral failure but an epistemological one: they did not have the Spirit; therefore they could not see what was there. The cross was, from the powers’ perspective, the elimination of a troublemaker; from God’s perspective, the salvation of the world. Same event, utterly different verdicts — because only one of those perspectives had the Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit (testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum). Calvin’s Institutes ground the believer’s certainty about Scripture not in external proofs but in the Spirit’s own witness to the heart. Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned; the Spirit of God alone can reveal them; the Spirit has been given to those who are in Christ. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos) is not merely unwilling but unable to receive spiritual things — a direct support for the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its noetic dimension.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for Apollos’s sophisticated rhetoric over Paul’s plain proclamation was, at root, a preference for a wisdom they could evaluate by their own natural capacities. Paul’s response: the real wisdom — the wisdom that saves — cannot be evaluated that way. It requires the Spirit to receive it. Now: The recurring temptation to evaluate the gospel by academic or cultural criteria — to ask whether Christianity can hold its own in the university seminar — misses Paul’s point. The knowledge of God is not the endpoint of human inquiry; it is the gift of the Spirit to the humble heart. This is why apologetics serves evangelism but cannot replace it: ultimately, only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory. None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul distinguishes two wisdoms: the wisdom of this age (passing away with it) and the wisdom of God (decreed before the ages). The first belongs to the rulers of this age — the powerful, the sophisticated, the theologically self-confident — who looked at Jesus of Nazareth and saw nothing worth preserving. The second is a hidden mystery, planned in eternity for the glory of those who receive it. “Lord of glory” — a title drawn from Psalm 24:7–10 — placed on the crucified Christ is one of the most startling christological statements in Paul: the One they nailed to a cross was the King of glory entering his own creation. The irony is cosmic in scale.

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The citation from Isaiah 64:4 (modified) describes the salvific blessings of the new age — the things God has been preparing from eternity for his people. Paul’s arresting claim: these things have been revealed. The future blessings remain future, but the knowledge of them, the grasp of God’s plan, the understanding of what he has done in Christ — this is already given to believers through the Spirit. “The Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” — not that the Spirit is investigating God as an inquirer, but that the Spirit has full access to God’s interior life as a member of the Godhead. And the Spirit who inhabits God’s depths has come to dwell in the believer.

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The analogy is precise: just as only your own spirit has access to your own thoughts, so only God’s Spirit has access to God’s thoughts. No amount of philosophical inquiry from outside can penetrate the divine interior life. But the believer has been given the Spirit — not the spirit of the world, which can access only worldly things, but the Spirit who is from God, who can therefore disclose what God has “freely given” (charisthenta — graced, given as gift). The knowledge of the gospel is itself gracious: not merely its content but the capacity to receive it is a gift of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual. The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The natural person” (psychikos anthrōpos) — the human being as constituted by natural birth alone, without the Spirit — cannot receive the things of the Spirit. The incapacity is double: does not accept (ou dechetai — will not, refuses) and is not able to understand (ou dynatai gnōnai — cannot, lacks the capacity). The inability is not purely intellectual; it is moral and spiritual. The fallen mind experiences the wisdom of the cross as foolishness — not because it is confused but because it is hostile to the God from whom it has turned. This is the noetic dimension of total depravity: sin distorts not only the will but the mind’s capacity to evaluate divine things rightly.

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one. “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The spiritual person — the one indwelt by the Spirit of God — has a capacity for evaluating reality that the natural person lacks. “Judges all things” does not mean omniscience but a Spirit-given discernment that penetrates beneath surface appearances to see things in their true relation to God. The citation from Isaiah 40:13 — “Who has understood the mind of the Lord?” — is answered with breathtaking boldness: “But we have the mind of Christ.” Not the totality of divine omniscience, but a real participation in Christ’s way of seeing — his priorities, his values, his interpretation of reality — given to the believer through the Spirit. This is the cognitive renewal that Paul later calls the renewing of the mind (Rom 12:2).

3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
Chapter 3 addresses the factional spirit at Corinth from a different angle: not the cross as criterion (ch. 1–2) but the nature of Christian ministry as criterion. The Corinthians are dividing over Paul and Apollos; Paul’s response is to describe what Paul and Apollos actually are in relation to each other and to God. They are co-workers in God’s field — one planting, one watering, but God alone giving the growth. They are builders on a single foundation, the only one that was ever laid: Jesus Christ.

The chapter escalates to its most searching moment in vv. 16–17: the Corinthian church is God’s temple, indwelt by God’s Spirit. This is not a private devotional truth but a corporate, ecclesiological one. The community together is the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit — and whoever destroys that community destroys the temple of God. The factional fights at Corinth are not merely social dysfunction; they are an assault on the dwelling place of God. Then the final movement (vv. 18–23) circles back to the theme of wisdom and boasting: stop boasting in men, because all things belong to you, and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul returns to the carnal condition of the Corinthians, now with more explicit diagnosis. They are not spiritual but fleshly — sarkinoi, made of flesh, still operating by the instincts of unregenerate human nature. The evidence? Jealousy and strife. These are not peripheral vices; in Paul’s catalogues of the works of the flesh (Gal 5:20), they sit alongside idolatry and sorcery. A church divided by personality loyalties is not merely socially dysfunctional; it is manifesting the symptoms of a life still dominated by the flesh rather than the Spirit.

The correction Paul offers is a radical redefinition of ministry. Paul planted, Apollos watered — but God gave the growth. Therefore “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth” (v. 7). This is not false modesty; it is precise theological description. The minister is the instrument; God is the cause. The Corinthians have been treating the instruments as if they were the cause, which is why their factions are so fierce. When you understand that Paul and Apollos are servants and God is the Lord, the competition between them collapses.

The image of God’s field introduces the first of two great metaphors in the chapter. Paul and Apollos are co-workers in one field that belongs to God — fellow labourers, not competitors. The competitive individualism of the Corinthian factions has imported the values of the Roman patronage system into the body of Christ; Paul refuses the framework entirely. “We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field, God’s building” (v. 9) — the transition to the second metaphor, the building, sets up the crucial passage that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated insistence that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is the Reformed doctrine of sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Paul preached; Apollos taught; but neither of them converted a single soul. Conversion is the work of God, not the achievement of the preacher. This means that the minister cannot take credit for results, cannot despair over apparent fruitlessness as if it were his own failure, and cannot be compared with another minister as if their different “results” reflected their different competencies. God gives where and when he wills.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions were measuring Paul and Apollos by their outputs — converts, rhetorical impact, visible results. Paul refuses this measuring rod: the results belong to God, not to the apostle. Now: The contemporary church is still tempted to evaluate ministry by attendance, conversion numbers, and cultural impact — and to attribute these to the skill and gifting of the human leader. Paul’s corrective: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God of growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready, for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul had been there two years earlier. They should have grown — but the jealousy and strife prove they have not. “Infants in Christ” is not condescension; it is diagnosis. The Corinthians pride themselves on their spiritual sophistication — their gifts, their knowledge, their theological factions — but their social behaviour betrays their actual spiritual age. This is one of the most searching tests Paul applies: spiritual maturity is not measured by the impressiveness of one’s spiritual experiences but by the quality of one’s love. A church full of spectacular gifts but riven by jealousy and strife is a church full of infants.

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What then is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Merely human” — the same word as “of the flesh.” Operating like unregenerate humans, by the world’s categories of status and competition. The rhetorical question “What then is Apollos? What then is Paul?” demolishes the faction leaders by answering: servants. Not masters, not authorities, not the objects of loyalty — servants. The Corinthians have inverted the hierarchy: they are treating servants as lords and the Lord as background. Paul and Apollos are defined by their function (through whom you believed) and their commission (as the Lord assigned) — both entirely derivative.

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary: The agricultural metaphor is simple and devastating. Planting and watering are real activities that require skill, effort, and faithfulness — Paul does not disparage them. But they are preparatory activities. The growth — the actual transformation of a seed into a plant — is entirely beyond the farmer’s power. The farmer can create conditions; he cannot create life. In the same way, Paul and Apollos can preach, teach, and pray — but the creation of spiritual life in a human soul is God’s exclusive act. “Are one” — united in purpose, not competing. And each will be rewarded according to their labour, not their results: faithfulness, not fruitfulness, is the standard of accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three possessives in rapid succession: God’s fellow workers, God’s field, God’s building. Ownership is the point. The ministers belong to God (not to the Corinthian factions); the church belongs to God (not to Paul or Apollos); the edifice being constructed belongs to God (not to the architect). The switch from “field” to “building” prepares for the extended metaphor that follows — and raises the stakes considerably. A field can be replanted; a building, once the foundation is laid, has a character determined by what is built on it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The building metaphor now unfolds with architectural precision and eschatological urgency. Paul is the master builder (arch&itekton) who laid the foundation; others build on it. But — and here is the point — the foundation was not Paul’s to choose. It was given: “no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (v. 11). The church is not free to choose its foundation. The only admissible foundation for a Christian community is Christ himself: his person, his work, his death and resurrection. Everything else — programmes, traditions, personalities, institutions — is superstructure, not foundation.

The materials used in superstructure are what will be tested: gold, silver, precious stones vs. wood, hay, straw. The test is fire — the eschatological judgment of the Last Day. Fire reveals what each minister’s work actually was: whether it was built on Christ, out of the resources of the gospel, for the glory of God (it survives); or whether it was built for human applause, institutional prestige, or personal empire (it burns). The minister whose work survives receives a reward; the minister whose work burns will be saved, “but only as through fire” — with nothing to show for his life’s work. This is not a passage about purgatory (as medieval theology read it) but about the accountability of Christian workers at the judgment.

Then the passage reaches its climax: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (v. 16). This is no longer about individual ministers but about the corporate community. The church together is the new temple — the place where the living God has chosen to dwell in the new covenant age. The Corinthian faction fights are therefore not merely unseemly; they are desecrating the dwelling place of God. “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him” (v. 17) is one of the most solemn warnings in the letter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

Paul’s identification of the church as God’s temple carries enormous theological weight in a letter written to a city famous for its pagan temples. The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the temple of Aphrodite; the city was saturated with temple culture, temple prostitution, and temple feasts. Paul’s claim is that the living God has abandoned temples made of stone and taken up residence in a community of people — flawed, fractious, sin-prone people — through his Spirit. The church is not a building where God may be found; the church is the people in whom God actually dwells. This is the new covenant fulfilment of every OT temple theology: God with his people, no longer mediated through architecture and ritual, but through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were not merely social dysfunction; they were a theological emergency. A fragmented community cannot be a temple — the architectural metaphor itself requires unity, all the stones fitting together. The faction wars were, quite literally, demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live. Now: Every church split, every faction, every deliberate destruction of community is an assault on the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. This gives a theological gravity to church unity that mere social concern cannot supply: we are not trying to be nice; we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “According to the grace of God given to me” — Paul identifies himself as master builder, but immediately locates the competency in grace, not skill. The foundation is not Paul’s achievement but God’s gift. And the warning “let each one take care how he builds” applies to every subsequent minister — teachers, leaders, preachers — who builds on what Paul laid. The non-negotiable: “no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.” Not Christ’s teachings alone, not Christian ethics, not Christian culture — the person and work of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen. Any ministry that shifts this foundation has not modified the building; it has destroyed it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast of materials is between the permanent and the combustible. Gold, silver, and precious stones survive fire; wood, hay, and straw are consumed by it. The Day — the Day of the Lord, the final judgment — is the test. What is meant by the quality of building? Fee argues it is the quality of the gospel content and the integrity of the method: teaching genuinely centred on Christ, building genuinely dependent on the Spirit, community genuinely shaped by love. Work built for human approval, institutional success, or rhetorical effect will burn. “Saved, but only as through fire” is vivid: the person escapes, but with nothing in his hands — like a man fleeing a burning house in his nightclothes. Salvation is secured; reward is lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Do you not know” — a formula Paul uses when he is appealing to something they should already understand. The “you” is plural throughout: you collectively, as a community, are the temple. The Holy Spirit’s indwelling is corporate before it is individual. And the warning is absolute: anyone who destroys this temple — through faction, immorality, false teaching, or divisive behaviour — faces divine destruction. This is not Paul being dramatic; it is Paul taking the holiness of God seriously. The God who struck down Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5) is the God who dwells in the Corinthian church. His temple is holy — and he will defend its holiness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes by circling back to the wisdom theme. “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise” (v. 18). The path to true wisdom runs through the humiliation of acknowledged folly — through the cross. This is not anti-intellectualism but a description of the epistemological conversion required: the person who comes to God thinking they have the resources to meet him on intellectual equal terms will leave empty; the person who comes in acknowledged poverty receives the wisdom of God as gift.

The citation from Job 5:13 and Psalm 94:11 — “He catches the wise in their craftiness” and “the Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” — ground the argument in Scripture’s own long testimony to the futility of human wisdom before God. Then the staggering positive conclusion: “all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future — all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.” The Corinthians have been fighting over which apostle to claim; Paul tells them they already own all the apostles, and all things, and they own them because they belong to Christ who owns everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from Him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great catalogue texts of what it means to be in Christ. Paul’s list — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present, future — is comprehensive: every apostle, every circumstance, every temporal horizon, even death itself, belongs to the believer in Christ. The Corinthians have been acting poor — squabbling over which apostle to claim — while they are infinitely rich. This is what Calvin called the “double grace” (“duplex gratia”) of union with Christ expanded to cosmic scope: the one who is in Christ owns, in principle, everything that Christ owns. They need not cling to Paul or Apollos; they have all of them, and infinitely more besides.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming one-quarter of the apostolic inheritance — “I follow Paul,” etc. — when they could have had the whole. Their factionalism was a self-imposed poverty in the middle of infinite wealth. Now: The Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing — claiming a slice when the whole belongs to him. The traditions are real and valuable; they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary: “Let him become a fool” — the path to divine wisdom requires the complete abandonment of confidence in one’s own intellectual resources. This is not a one-time act but a posture — the ongoing willingness to submit one’s categories to the word of the cross rather than evaluating the cross by one’s categories. The Job and Psalm citations demonstrate that God’s attitude to human wisdom has been consistent across the canon: he catches the clever in their own cleverness; he sees through the sophisticated plans to the futility beneath. The wisdom that imagines it can approach God on its own terms is the wisdom that will be most surprised on the day it meets him.

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future— all are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary: The cascade of “all things are yours” is breathtaking in its scope. Every apostle’s ministry belongs to the whole church; no one faction has a private claim on Paul or on Apollos. The world itself — the created order, history, the cosmos — belongs to those who are in Christ (cf. Rom 8:17; Heb 2:5). Life and death are both theirs — meaning neither has a claim on them that Christ cannot override. Present and future — no moment escapes the ownership of Christ’s people. And then the grounding chain: you are Christ’s (by belonging, by union), and Christ is God’s (by eternal Sonship). The cosmic inheritance flows from the relationship: because Christ owns all things as the Son of God, and because you belong to Christ, all things are yours. Faction over apostles is absurd: you already own all of them.

4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the most personal of the opening section’s chapters — Paul at his most tender and most fierce. He describes the apostolic calling as stewardship: apostles are servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, accountable not to the Corinthian audience but to the Lord who will judge on the Last Day. The Corinthians have been sitting in judgment on Paul and Apollos — evaluating their performance, weighing their merits, forming factions around their preferences. Paul challenges this from every direction: the only judge who matters has not yet rendered his verdict, and that verdict will contain surprises.

Then the chapter turns, and Paul describes what apostleship actually looks like from the inside: the apostles are a spectacle to the world, last of all, condemned to death. While the Corinthians have become kings, filled, rich, they are hungry, thirsty, poorly dressed, reviled, homeless, the scum of the world. The irony is devastating. The church that has modelled itself on the world’s standards of success looks at the apostles — weak, despised, suffering — and fails to recognise them as the authentic embodiment of the gospel they profess. Chapter 4 ends with a father’s appeal: I am not writing this to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children. Imitate me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The proper way to think about Paul and Apollos is not as competing spiritual celebrities but as servants (hypēretas — literally, under-rowers, the galley slaves at the bottom of the ship) and stewards. A steward administers someone else’s property; he has no claim on it and no right to use it for personal enrichment. His one qualification is faithfulness. This single word — “it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (v. 2) — is the only criterion Paul acknowledges for apostolic evaluation. Not brilliance, not fruitfulness, not cultural impact: faithfulness.

The passage then moves into one of Paul’s most striking statements of judicial humility. He is aware of no charge against himself (v. 4) — but this does not acquit him. The judge is the Lord. Paul refuses to sit in judgment on himself because the final verdict belongs to the One who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart. The day of judgment will not merely evaluate actions; it will disclose motivations. Everything hidden — including the hidden pride and self-interest that can lurk beneath apparently faithful ministry — will be brought into the light.

Verse 7 then aims a dart with surgical precision at the root of Corinthian pride: “For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?” Three questions that leave the Corinthian boaster nowhere to hide. Every gift, every capacity, every spiritual experience is received — given by grace, not earned by merit. To boast in received gifts is to claim credit for a gift, which is both ingratitude and dishonesty.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatological Judgment and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pre-judge himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism but eschatological realism. The final judgment has not yet been rendered; therefore all present judgments — including self-assessment — are provisional. Reformed theology has always warned against both false confidence (I know I am right) and false despair (I know I am condemned): both pre-empt the judgment that belongs to God alone. The practical implication is freedom: neither to be destroyed by human criticism nor to be puffed up by human praise, because neither the critic nor the flatterer is the judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were evaluating Paul and finding him wanting, not by the standard of faithfulness but by the standards of rhetorical eloquence and visible success. Paul refuses the evaluation: you are not my judge; the Lord is. Now: Ministry evaluation by attendance, public approval, or conference invitations is the contemporary equivalent. The minister who structures his ministry around what will get him praised by his peers has already chosen the wrong judge. The only evaluation that matters is the Lord’s — and it will assess what the heart actually was.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary: “This is how one should regard us” — Paul is correcting the Corinthian lens. The correct category is not “my apostle” vs. “your apostle” but “servants” and “stewards” — both terms defined by subordination, not status. A servant serves his master’s agenda; a steward administers his master’s property. The “mysteries of God” are not esoteric secrets but the once-hidden, now-revealed gospel of Christ crucified (cf. 2:7). The apostles are entrusted with this treasure, not as owners but as administrators. The one qualification for this administration is faithfulness — not brilliance, not fruitfulness, not popularity. Faithfulness to the message as received.

verseByVerse.quote: But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court. In fact, I do not even judge myself. For I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted. It is the Lord who judges me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul’s detachment from human judgment is not arrogance but theological clarity. Human courts — including the court of his own conscience — cannot issue the verdict that matters. His clear conscience is not innocence but limitation: his self-knowledge is partial, his self-assessment possibly mistaken. “The Lord who judges me” — ho de anakrinōn me kyrios estin — is the only judge before whom all evidence is available and all motivation transparent. This is one of the most liberating statements in the NT for Christian ministry: you do not need to manage your reputation, because the only judge who matters sees through all reputation management to what you actually are.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God. I have applied all these things to myself and Apollos for your benefit, brothers, that you may learn by us not to go beyond what is written, that none of you may be puffed up in favor of one against another.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Before the time” — the premature verdict, issued before all the evidence is in, is both presumptuous and premature. The Last Day will bring to light not only actions but “the purposes of the heart” — the motivations, the interior driving forces, the things hidden even from the actor himself. The commendation — singular — will come from God: not from the congregation, not from the conference circuit, not from peer review. Paul applies this to himself and Apollos as an object lesson: stop choosing sides between them, because neither of them has been evaluated yet, and when they are, it will not be by Corinthian criteria.

verseByVerse.quote: For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?
verseByVerse.commentary: The three questions are relentless. The first asks: what distinguishes you from anyone else? The implication: nothing that is not a gift of God. The second: what have you that was not given? The answer is nothing — not intelligence, not spiritual gifts, not faith itself. The third is the logical consequence: boasting in received gifts is incoherent. This verse is the theological heart of sola gratia in its social application: the person who boasts in spiritual gifts is claiming credit for charity they received and never earned. Keller calls this the “grace question” — when you feel superior to another Christian, ask: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Apostles as Spectacle: The Cruciform Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Here Paul employs one of his sharpest rhetorical weapons: sustained, ironic contrast. “Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you!” (v. 8). The irony is biting and precise. The Corinthians have already achieved, in their own minds, the eschatological glory that belongs to the resurrection age — the riches, the reigning, the fulfilment. But the resurrection has not yet come; Christ has not yet returned; the kingdom has not yet been consummated. Their triumphalism is a premature arrival in a future that is not yet.

The contrast Paul draws is between the Corinthian experience of glory and the apostolic experience of cruciformity. Apostles are last, condemned to death, made a spectacle. While they reign, the apostles are hungry, thirsty, poorly dressed, brutally treated, homeless. While they are honoured, the apostles are reviled, persecuted, slandered. While they are wise, the apostles are fools for Christ’s sake. The pattern is deliberate: the apostolic life is shaped by the cross, not the resurrection. This age — between the first and second coming — is the age of bearing the cross, not wearing the crown.

Paul’s concluding summary is brutal: “We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things” (v. 13). Perikatharmata and peripsēma both connote the filth scraped from a surface — what is cleaned off and discarded. This is how Paul describes his apostolic credentials. Not miracles (though he has those), not visions (though he has those too), but the marks of a life shaped by the dying of Jesus. The cross is not merely Paul’s theology; it is his biography.
verseByVerse.theology:
Realized Eschatology and the Cross-Shaped Life

The Corinthians’ problem was not merely social pride but theological confusion about which age they were in. They were living as if the resurrection age had fully arrived — treating this present life as the time of reigning and riches. Paul’s corrective is eschatological: we are still in the “between the times,” the age between the first and second coming, in which the pattern of the Christian life is cruciform, not triumphant. The “not yet” of eschatology shapes the “how” of Christian living. Suffering, weakness, and apparent defeat are not failures of faith but participation in Christ’s own pattern — the pattern of resurrection that comes through, not around, the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman spectacle of condemned criminals paraded before the crowd before their execution is the image behind v. 9 (“made a spectacle”). Paul uses the imagery of the arena: God has made the apostles last, like the condemned criminals brought on at the end of the show. This was not hyperbole; Paul had been beaten, imprisoned, and would eventually be executed. Now: The prosperity gospel is the contemporary version of Corinthian triumphalism: the claim that health, wealth, and success are the normal marks of Spirit-filled Christianity. Paul’s fools for Christ’s sake, hungry and homeless, are a permanent rebuke to any theology that makes suffering an anomaly rather than a participation in the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And would that you did reign, so that we might share the rule with you! For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men. We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are held in honor, but we in disrepute.
