verseByVerse.commentary: The triple “already” of Corinthian triumphalism is met by Paul’s triple contrast: apostles as fools, weak, in disrepute; Corinthians as wise, strong, honoured. The contrast is not Paul being bitter; it is Paul being diagnostic. The Corinthians have achieved a social respectability that the cross-bearing apostle has not — and this, Paul implies, should give them pause. If the pattern of authentic Christianity is cruciform, why are the Corinthians doing so well? The “spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men” echoes the arena imagery: the apostles are the condemned criminals paraded before the universe. And they accept this — as the logical expression of preaching a crucified Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things.
verseByVerse.commentary: The list is concrete, physical, and present tense (“to the present hour”). Paul is not describing past sufferings but his current condition. The responses to ill-treatment — blessing, endurance, entreaty — are not stoic fortitude but cruciform love: the pattern of Jesus before Pilate, of the servant who did not retaliate, of the one who prayed “Father, forgive them.” “Scum of the world, refuse of all things” — the strongest possible social degradation, deliberately claimed by the apostle as his credentials. The man who can describe his ministry in these terms is the man who has understood what he preaches: that the wisdom and power of God are found in weakness and folly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — A Father’s Warning and Appeal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The irony drops. Paul’s tone shifts from sharp to tender: “I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children” (v. 14). The whole chapter — the biting contrasts, the withering irony — was not the anger of an offended ego but the grief of a father watching his children go wrong. Paul is not competing with the Corinthians; he loves them. He is their father in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The implication is not that Paul has authority over them as a tyrant but that he has a claim on their hearts as a parent — and a parent’s deepest desire is not obedience but flourishing.

The appeal to imitate Paul (v. 16) is not arrogant. In a world without books, seminaries, or theological education, the primary vehicle of pastoral formation was the imitation of a living model. Paul is offering himself — specifically the pattern of cruciform ministry described in vv. 8–13 — as the template for what gospel living looks like. Timothy is being sent as Paul’s representative precisely to remind them of Paul’s ways in Christ: not his opinions but his life-pattern.

The chapter ends with a warning that reintroduces the note of apostolic authority. Some at Corinth have become arrogant, imagining that Paul will not come to deal with them. He will come — and when he does, he will find out not the talk of the arrogant but their power. The kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. Paul will come with love and a gentle spirit — if they will receive it. If not, he will come with a rod. The father’s love is real; so is the father’s authority.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fatherhood of the Apostle and Spiritual Formation by Imitation

Paul’s claim to spiritual fatherhood over the Corinthian church is grounded in the gospel: “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (v. 15). The new birth produces a spiritual parentage — and the one through whose proclamation the Spirit brought new birth to a community is, in a real sense, their spiritual father. This is not about control but about formation. Calvin, commenting on v. 16, noted that Paul asks to be imitated not as an authority but as a living embodiment of the gospel he preached: “He calls them to imitate not his person but his pattern — the pattern of the cross.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had, in Paul’s absence, developed arrogant teachers who had dismissed the apostle. Timothy is sent to embody what Paul had taught by his life — because argument alone, without the living example, is insufficient. Now: The pastoral call to “imitate me as I imitate Christ” (11:1) is the most demanding thing a minister can say — and the most necessary. Disciples need models, not merely doctrines. The church that produces only correct theology without cruciform character has missed the point of the apostolic office.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children. For though you have countless guides in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel. I urge you, then, be imitators of me.
verseByVerse.commentary: The distinction between guides (paidagōgous) and father is important in the ancient world: the paidagogos was the household slave who escorted children to school and ensured their basic education — a functionary, not a parent. Paul is not disparaging other teachers but claiming a different kind of relationship: the one who mediates new birth has a bond with the spiritual children that no subsequent teacher can replicate. The call to imitation is therefore not a power play but an appeal to origin: remember who I was to you when I was weak and trembling; the life I lived then is the life I am calling you back to.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why I sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, to remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach them everywhere in every church. Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you. But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power.
verseByVerse.commentary: Timothy is sent not as Paul’s substitute but as Paul’s incarnate reminder — “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” who embodies by his own life the pattern Paul has been describing. “My ways in Christ” are not merely doctrines but practices: the whole way of being a Christian that Paul lives and teaches in every church. The “arrogant” — ephysiothesan, puffed up — who imagine Paul is absent and therefore controllable will be surprised. Paul will come — Lord willing — and he will not be assessing their rhetorical ability but their actual spiritual power: the power of a life transformed by the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power. What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?
verseByVerse.commentary: “The kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power” — a statement that cuts both ways. It rebukes the Corinthian talkers who mistake sophisticated discourse for spiritual substance; and it grounds Paul’s own claim to power not in rhetorical performance but in the Spirit-wrought transformation of lives. The final question — rod or love in gentleness? — is the question of every parent to a wayward child. The rod is not vindictiveness but discipline; the gentleness is not weakness but preference. Paul desperately wants to come gently. The response is in the Corinthians’ hands: repent of the arrogance, receive the apostle, and the father arrives; persist in pride, and the father arrives with the rod.

5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Chapter 5 confronts the most scandalous pastoral failure in the letter: a man is living openly with his father’s wife — a sexual relationship forbidden by both Roman law and the Torah — and the church is not only tolerating it but apparently celebrating their openness and inclusivity. Paul is appalled, not merely by the sin itself but by the community’s response to it: pride. They are “puffed up” (v. 2) when they ought to be mourning. The church that boasts in its spiritual gifts and theological sophistication has somehow become the kind of community that treats gross immorality as evidence of its broad-mindedness.

Paul’s response is a theology of church discipline rooted in the holiness of God and the meaning of the cross. The community that tolerates unrepentant sin is like unleavened bread with a lump of leaven in it: the whole loaf is compromised. Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb; therefore the community that shelters in that sacrifice must be a community of sincere integrity, not malice and evil. The exclusion of the unrepentant sinner from the community is not revenge but surgery — and not merely for the community’s sake but for the sinner’s: “that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord” (v. 5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The opening accusation is stark: “It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans — for a man has his father’s wife.” The relationship would have violated both Mosaic law (Lev 18:8; Deut 22:30) and Roman legal norms. It was not merely sinful by Christian standards but scandalous by the standards of the surrounding culture. And the church was proud of it — perhaps viewing their non-judgmental acceptance of the relationship as evidence of their spiritual sophistication and gospel freedom.

Paul’s verdict is delivered with apostolic authority. As already present in spirit, he has already judged: the man is to be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. This extraordinary phrase — “delivered to Satan” — means exclusion from the community of God’s people into the domain where Satan holds sway. The intention is not punitive but redemptive: “that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.” Church discipline, rightly understood, is not the church washing its hands of a sinner but performing a painful surgery designed to bring him to his senses before the Last Day.

The Passover metaphor is the theological engine of the passage. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. The Passover required the complete removal of all leaven from the household before the feast — a single lump of yeast, left in place, works through the whole batch. The community that allows tolerated immorality to remain is a Passover household with leaven in the pantry: the sacrifice has been made, but the household is not living in correspondence with it. “Let us celebrate the festival...with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (v. 8) — the ongoing moral life of the community should match the purity that the Passover sacrifice purchased.
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

The Reformed tradition has always identified church discipline as one of the marks of the true church (alongside Word and sacraments). Calvin’s Institutes III.11–14 ground discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the holiness of the community is not a human achievement but a participation in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the final word against the sinner but the penultimate word, designed to produce repentance. The church that refuses to discipline its members — in the name of grace, tolerance, or avoiding conflict — is, paradoxically, acting without grace: it is allowing the leavening of unrepentant sin to compromise the whole community and denying the sinner the painful mercy of confrontation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian pride in tolerating this relationship may reflect the influence of the “strong” in the community — those with social status and rhetorical sophistication who had reinterpreted gospel freedom as moral permissiveness. The man involved may have been a patron of the church, someone whose loss the community feared. Paul overrides all such calculations: the gospel has higher priorities than keeping wealthy members comfortable. Now: The contemporary church’s allergy to any form of discipline is well-documented and widely lamented. Churches afraid to confront unrepentant sin in their members have, ironically, become communities shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Actually” — Paul emphasises the reality because the Corinthians seem to have normalised something that should have caused universal alarm. “Not tolerated even among pagans” is precise: Roman law forbade marriage between a man and his stepmother. The community is exhibiting the wrong emotion entirely: pride instead of mourning. The grief Paul calls for is not merely sorrow about the sin but the mourning of a community that has lost something precious — its integrity, its corporate holiness, its correspondence with the gospel it confesses. The remedy is removal: not excommunication as an expression of contempt but surgical separation for the sake of both community and sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus, you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul’s apostolic judgment is not tentative but certain: “I have already pronounced.” The assembly in the name of the Lord Jesus is the gathering of the community with Christ’s own authority present — not a church business meeting but an act of the body of Christ acting with Christ’s power. “Delivered to Satan” most likely means exclusion from the protective sphere of the Christian community into the world where Satan operates — the domain of illness, suffering, and death that results from separation from God’s grace. The “destruction of the flesh” may refer to the death of fleshly sinful desires, or to physical suffering, or both — but the end is redemptive: that the spirit may be saved. The judgment is pastoral before it is punitive.

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Passover theology is breathtaking in its compression. Christ has been sacrificed as the Passover Lamb — the one whose blood, applied to the doorposts of the community, causes death to pass over. But a Passover household in which the leavening agent of immorality is left in place is a contradiction. The indicative drives the imperative: “you really are unleavened” (because of Christ’s sacrifice) — “therefore cleanse out the old leaven.” You are what you are called to become. The moral life is not a performance to win status but a correspondence to a reality already established by the cross. The “old leaven of malice and evil” stands against “sincerity and truth” — not a minor social preference but the difference between a community shaped by the cross and one still shaped by the flesh.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A clarification that Paul has apparently already needed to make once before (v. 9: “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people”). The Corinthians had apparently applied this to the world at large, concluding that they must withdraw from every immoral person in Corinth — which would have required leaving the world entirely. Paul corrects the misunderstanding with characteristic precision: the command applies to those inside the community who name the name of Christ and live in unrepentant immorality, not to unbelievers outside who make no such profession.

The logic is powerful: God judges those outside the community; the community is responsible to judge those inside. The world cannot be held to the standard of the gospel it has not received; the church member who has received the gospel and persists in unrepentant wickedness has abandoned the correspondence between profession and life that the gospel demands. To refuse judgment on such a person is not grace but confusion — treating the unrepentant church member as if they were the unbelieving neighbour.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside the community (v. 12–13) defines the scope of church discipline with precision. The church is not called to police the world; it is called to maintain the integrity of its own fellowship. “God judges those outside” — this is not indifference to the world’s sin but a recognition that the church is not the world’s court of law. The church’s mission to the world is evangelism, not judgment; its internal discipline is precisely what enables it to be a credible witness in the world it is trying to reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. Misapplied teaching on holiness tends in two directions: either becoming a withdrawal sect (refusing all contact with sinful unbelievers) or collapsing into permissiveness (refusing all internal accountability). The Corinthians had done the latter. Now: The same confusion persists: churches that are either socially withdrawn from the world (failing at evangelism) or internally undisciplined (failing at community). Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world. But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler— not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary: The precision of “who bears the name of brother” is decisive. The non-association Paul commands is not social quarantine of unbelievers but the withholding of table fellowship from a professing Christian living in unrepentant wickedness. “Not even to eat with such a one” — eating together in the ancient world was an expression of shared life and mutual acceptance. To eat with an unrepentant sinner is to signal that his sin is no obstacle to full fellowship, which is a lie about both the gospel and about the love the sinner needs. The list of disqualifying sins is broad: sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, reviling, drunkenness, swindling — covering the whole range of the vices that characterise life without the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary: The closing citation from Deuteronomy (17:7; 19:19; 22:21–24) places Paul’s instruction in the tradition of Israel’s covenant community maintaining its purity before God. “Purge the evil person” in Israel meant execution of the physically threatening; in the new covenant community it means exclusion from fellowship. The purpose is identical: to protect the community’s correspondence with its covenanting God. “God judges those outside” is not a statement of indifference to unbelievers’ sin but a recognition that their accountability is to God directly, not mediated through the church’s internal discipline. The church’s task toward them is proclamation, not policing.

6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Chapter 6 addresses two more symptoms of the same disease: the Corinthians’ preference for the world’s courts over the community’s wisdom, and their confusion about what gospel freedom means in the domain of the body. The two sections are linked by the common thread of what it means that the Holy Spirit dwells in the believer — individually and corporately. If the Spirit of the living God inhabits these people, then taking one another before pagan courts is an absurd undervaluation of the wisdom God has given the community, and using the body for sexual immorality is an act of desecration against the temple of God.

The chapter reaches its climax in one of the most electrifying declarations in all of Paul: “Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” The body is not a neutral instrument for satisfying appetites; it is the dwelling place of the Spirit of the Creator. The resurrection of Christ, which will raise this same body, makes the body eternally significant. The cross, which purchased this body at infinite cost, makes the body not our own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s opening is blunt: “Does anyone of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints?” The church at Corinth — spiritually gifted, theologically sophisticated — was taking its internal disputes to pagan magistrates. Paul finds this not merely improper but absurd and shameful. The community that will one day judge the world and the angels is incapable of settling a trivial lawsuit?

The critique has two edges. The first: the church has the wisdom and authority to resolve internal disputes — and refusing to use it is a failure of community life. The second: the very existence of such lawsuits is itself a defeat. Even if the church could resolve every dispute with perfect fairness, the fact that brothers are suing brothers rather than suffering wrong and accepting being defrauded reveals a fundamental absence of the cruciform character the gospel produces. The person shaped by the cross willingly absorbs loss for the sake of the brother; the Corinthian litigant insists on his rights at the expense of the community.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul’s argument from eschatology — “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2) — is a characteristic move: the future reality of the believer’s status shapes present behaviour. The saints who will participate in Christ’s eschatological judgment (Dan 7:22; Rev 20:4) have already, in their union with Christ, been granted a dignity that makes recourse to pagan courts for petty disputes absurd. The inconsistency Paul exposes is not merely practical but theological: why would those destined for cosmic judicial authority submit their neighbourhood disputes to judges who do not acknowledge Christ?
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Going to court was not merely a legal act but a social strategy. Paul refuses the framework: the cross creates a community in which the willingness to absorb loss is a greater display of power than the ability to win in court. Now: The Christian instinct to reach for legal remedies when wronged by a fellow believer is understandable but reveals how deeply the world’s categories of justice and self-protection have shaped us. Paul’s question — “Why not rather suffer wrong?” — is among the most countercultural sentences in the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary: “The unrighteous” for pagan judges is not a slur but a theological description: those who do not have the righteousness of Christ and therefore cannot judge by his standards. The eschatological argument escalates to the cosmic: those who will judge angels — presumably the fallen angels who are reserved for judgment (2 Pet 2:4; Jude 6) — are surely competent to decide property disputes and financial disagreements. The irony is layered: the Corinthians are proud of their spiritual status while demeaning their spiritual competence by outsourcing their disputes to people of lower standing in the economy of God.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame. Can it be that there is no one among you wise enough to settle a dispute between the brothers, but brother goes to law against brother, and that before unbelievers?
verseByVerse.commentary: “I say this to your shame” — Paul rarely uses this phrase; when he does, the rebuke is serious. A church that boasts of gifts, wisdom, and spiritual knowledge cannot find a single wise person to adjudicate an internal dispute? The shame is not merely about the legal strategy but about the community’s failure to become what the gospel calls it to be: a community of Spirit-formed wisdom capable of managing its own internal life. “Before unbelievers” — the public spectacle of Christians fighting each other in court is, additionally, a testimony disaster: the watching world sees a community that cannot live at peace with itself.

verseByVerse.quote: To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? But you yourselves wrong and defraud— even your own brothers!
verseByVerse.commentary: “Already a defeat” — even before the verdict is rendered, the existence of the lawsuit is a loss. The community that produces lawsuits between brothers has already failed at something more important than the disputed property. “Why not rather suffer wrong?” — this echoes the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5:39–40) and the cross itself: the Lord of glory absorbed infinite wrong without retaliation. The person formed by the cross has a different calculus about rights and losses: the relationship with the brother is worth more than the disputed sum. The final turn — “you yourselves wrong and defraud” — is the most damning observation: they are not merely failing to absorb wrong but actively inflicting it on fellow believers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The Unrighteous Will Not Inherit the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Between the lawsuit passage and the sexuality passage, Paul inserts a solemn catalogue of sins that exclude from the kingdom of God. The list is not a complete inventory of all possible disqualifying sins but a selection of the specific patterns that characterise Corinthian culture: sexual immorality, idolatry, adultery, homosexual behaviour, theft, greed, drunkenness, reviling, swindling. The community must not be deceived: these things exclude from the kingdom.

But the thunderclap of v. 11 follows immediately: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” Three passive verbs, three completed divine acts: washed, sanctified, justified. The people in the community who once practised these things have been transformed — not by self-improvement but by divine action in the name of Christ and through the Spirit. The catalogue of vices is not a present description but a past one: “such were some of you.” The past tense is the gospel’s answer to shame.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification, Sanctification, and the New Identity

The triad of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — covers the full scope of soteric transformation. Reformed theology typically orders justification before sanctification logically; Paul here places sanctification before justification in the list, which suggests he is not giving a logical order but a rhetorical one: moving from the most experientially tangible (washing, cleansing from the pollution of past sin) to the most legally decisive (justification, right standing before God). All three are accomplished “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — trinitarian to the root.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in vv. 9–10 describes the Corinthian street — not foreign or distant behaviour but the lives many of the congregation had lived and from which the gospel had extracted them. Paul is not writing to people who need to be warned away from exotic sins; he is reminding them of who they used to be, so they understand what they now are. Now: The church in every generation contains people whose past is on the list in vv. 9–10. The three words of v. 11 — washed, sanctified, justified — are the most liberating words any of them will ever hear about that past. It was real; the transformation is realer.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who practice homosexuality, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor swindlers will inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Do not be deceived” — the deception Paul warns against is the comfortable assumption that one can persist in these patterns while inheriting the kingdom. The list is selective and socially specific: these are the sins most visibly present in the Corinthian community and its surrounding culture. “Inherit the kingdom” is not merely “go to heaven” but participation in the full eschatological flourishing of God’s new creation. The warning is serious but not despairing: Paul is writing to people who have been transformed, reminding them that the transformation is real and the new identity is not compatible with the old pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Such were some of you” — the aorist tense is irreversible: this is past, completed, over. The three passive verbs describe what God did to them: washed (the pollution of sin removed, probably evoking baptism), sanctified (set apart, consecrated to God, belonging to his sphere), justified (declared righteous, standing acquitted before the divine Judge). The double agency — “in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” — grounds the entire transformation in trinitarian action. No human effort produced these results; divine initiative accomplished them. The past tense is not a boast but a liberation: whatever is on that list in vv. 9–10, it is past, dealt with, cancelled by the blood of Christ and the work of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — Flee Sexual Immorality: The Body as Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter’s theological climax addresses the use of the body and does so through two competing slogans — slogans that some Corinthians were apparently using to justify sexual behaviour. “All things are lawful for me” (v. 12) was likely a Corinthian slogan rooted in a misunderstanding of Christian freedom: if Christ has freed us from the law, then there are no restrictions on the body. “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food” (v. 13) was the Corinthian argument for sexual indulgence: the body is a biological instrument with natural appetites; satisfying those appetites with a prostitute is no more significant than eating a meal.

Paul demolishes both slogans with theology. The body is not a neutral instrument for appetite satisfaction; it is the member of Christ, destined for resurrection, indwelt by the Holy Spirit. To take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute is to bring Christ himself into that union — because the believer is one spirit with the Lord (v. 17). The body that will be raised from the dead is the same body that is now misused; the body indwelt by the Holy Spirit is the body now being treated as a commodity.

The climax is unforgettable: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” The price was the cross — the blood of Christ. The body, bought at that price, does not belong to the believer to use as he pleases. It belongs to God, as a temple belongs to its deity — and what is done in a temple is done in the presence of, and for the honour of, the one who inhabits it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection and the Significance of the Body

Paul’s argument for sexual ethics is grounded in resurrection theology: “God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power” (v. 14). The body is not a temporary shell to be discarded but the vehicle of the self that God will raise — the same body, transformed. This is why what we do with the body matters eternally. The body-soul dualism that dismisses bodily sins as theologically insignificant — a common Gnostic error in the ancient world — is precisely what Paul is refuting. The resurrection of the body is the theological foundation of a robust, embodied Christian ethics.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Visiting a temple prostitute in Corinth was a normal feature of social and religious life — not perceived as transgression but as participation in the city’s religious and social fabric. The Corinthian with a “strong” theology might have regarded it as religiously meaningless (the idol is nothing) and biologically natural. Paul’s counter-argument changes the frame entirely: it is not religiously meaningless because the Holy Spirit inhabits the believer’s body; the body is not yours to give away because it was bought with a price. Now: The sexual ethics of any age are shaped by whatever account it gives of the body. Paul’s account — the body as Spirit-indwelt, resurrection-destined, cross-purchased — is the most exalted account of human physicality in any worldview.

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful for me,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful for me,” but I will not be dominated by anything. “Food is meant for the stomach and the stomach for food”— and God will destroy both one and the other. The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul appears to cite and then correct Corinthian slogans. “All things are lawful” — Paul does not entirely reject this; Christian freedom is real. But freedom is not the only category: helpfulness and self-mastery also matter. “I will not be dominated by anything” — the person who uses sexual freedom as their justification for sleeping with prostitutes is, by that very fact, dominated by their appetites, which is a new form of slavery. “Food and the stomach” argument Paul refuses entirely: the analogy breaks down because food is a morally neutral biological function, while sex involves the whole person in a union that carries permanent significance (vv. 16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Never!
verseByVerse.commentary: The resurrection argument is decisive: God who raised Christ will raise us — bodily, physically, the same flesh in transformed form. If that is true, then the body has an eschatological destiny; it is not a temporary vehicle to be used up and discarded. “Members of Christ” — the body of the believer is already, by union with Christ, a part of Christ’s own body. To take those members — which belong to Christ — and unite them with a prostitute is not merely personal sin but a violation of the union with Christ. “Never!” (mē genoito — may it never be!) is the strongest negative in Paul’s rhetorical repertoire.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, “The two will become one flesh.” But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Genesis 2:24 citation is the devastating move: sexual union is not merely a physical transaction but the creation of a “one flesh” bond — a union of persons, not merely bodies. This was always true; the gospel makes it eschatologically momentous. The believer who is “joined to the Lord” (kollōmenos — same verb as “joined to a prostitute”) is one spirit with Christ. These two unions — with Christ and with a prostitute — are not merely incompatible preferences; they are an ontological contradiction. The person cannot be at once the single spirit with the Lord that union with Christ creates and the one flesh with a prostitute that sexual union creates.

verseByVerse.quote: Flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Flee” — not engage, not argue with, not manage: flee. The urgency of the imperative reflects the seriousness of the danger. “Sins against his own body” — whatever the precise meaning (interpreters debate it), the point is that sexual sin has an immediacy and intimacy of self-damage that other sins do not: the whole self, body and spirit together, is implicated in a way that distinguishes it from other vices. Then the climax: the body is the temple of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit who once filled the Jerusalem temple now inhabits the bodies of believers — individually and corporately. “You are not your own” — the most liberating words ever spoken to a self that has been destroying itself with false freedom. You were bought: the cross purchased you. You belong to God: glorify him in the body he redeemed.

7.title: Marriage, Celibacy, and the Calling of God
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is Paul’s most extended treatment of marriage, and it has been misread in every generation. It is not an argument for celibacy as the spiritually superior state, nor a concession to physical weakness, nor an expression of sexual pessimism. It is a carefully calibrated pastoral response to a specific set of questions from the Corinthian church, shaped throughout by two governing convictions: the nearness of the end (“the present form of this world is passing away,” v. 31) and the principle that each person should remain in the calling in which they were called (v. 17, 20, 24).

Paul affirms marriage fully: the husband and wife have mutual obligations to one another; neither may withhold from the other except by mutual agreement for prayer; divorce is forbidden (with one exception). He also affirms celibacy as a genuine gift from God — not a higher state but a different calling that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord. The practical advice throughout is shaped by the eschatological pressure: given the compressed nature of this age, those already in a status (married, single, slave, free) should generally remain there, serving the Lord as they are, rather than treating a change of status as a spiritual upgrade.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens by responding to a Corinthian slogan: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” Some at Corinth, apparently influenced by an ascetic theology that treated the body as spiritually inferior, had concluded that even within marriage sexual relations were to be avoided. Paul corrects this without simply contradicting it: yes, celibacy is good — but precisely because sexual desire is real, marriage is the God-given context for its fulfilment, and within marriage, mutual obligation is the governing principle.

The language of “authority” in vv. 3–4 is strikingly mutual: the husband has authority over his wife’s body, and she over his. In a culture where the husband’s authority was assumed and the wife’s was unthinkable, Paul’s symmetry is remarkable. Neither partner owns their own body exclusively; each belongs to the other. The practical implication — do not deprive each other except by mutual consent for a limited time of prayer — takes seriously both the goodness of sexual life in marriage and the value of devoted prayer.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goodness of Marriage and the Gift of Celibacy

Reformed theology has always resisted the Catholic elevation of celibacy above marriage as the spiritually superior state. Calvin read 1 Corinthians 7 as affirming both callings as genuine gifts of God, neither intrinsically superior. Luther’s own marriage was a theological act — a public demonstration that marriage is not a second-class spiritual status. Paul’s careful handling of both callings in vv. 7–9 supports this reading: celibacy is a charisma, a grace-gift, as is marriage. Neither is commanded; both are honoured.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian ascetics who were advocating celibacy within marriage may have been influenced by the same Gnostic-adjacent body-negativity that produced the “food for the stomach” argument in chapter 6 — but in the opposite direction: if the body is spiritually inferior, why give it what it desires? Paul’s answer refuses both the libertine and the ascetic extremes. Now: The Christian tradition has tended to err in one direction or the other in every generation: either treating sexuality as a dangerous force to be suppressed, or (more recently) treating it as a sovereign identity that cannot be questioned. Paul’s account makes it neither: a good gift, shaped by covenant obligation, eschatologically relativised.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.
verseByVerse.commentary: The opening “now concerning” (peri de) signals Paul’s response to a specific question from the Corinthians’ letter. Whether v. 1b is a Corinthian slogan Paul is about to qualify, or Paul’s own opening position, scholars debate — the grammatical evidence leans toward quoting the Corinthians. Either way, Paul immediately qualifies: given the reality of sexual temptation, the proper context for sexual life is the exclusive, committed bond of marriage. “Each man his own wife, each woman her own husband” — the symmetry is deliberate: the obligations and protections of marriage apply equally to both partners.

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you through your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary: The mutuality here is revolutionary in its context. Roman marriage gave the husband virtually all legal and social authority; Paul’s insistence on the wife’s authority over the husband’s body as the exact counterpart to his authority over hers was genuinely countercultural. The body in marriage is not one’s private property to withhold; it is given — in something that echoes, at the creaturely level, the mutual self-giving of the Trinity. The exception — mutual consent, limited time, prayer — affirms the spiritual disciplines of marriage while refusing to make them an excuse for the unilateral withdrawal that the Corinthian ascetics apparently practiced.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another. To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Each has his own gift from God” — both marriage and celibacy are charismata: grace-gifts, not personal achievements. Paul wishes others could share his contentment in singleness but does not command it because he cannot command a gift. The phrase “burn with passion” is graphic: the word suggests being consumed, ablaze with desire that cannot be righteously satisfied. Marriage is not a spiritual failure for those who burn; it is the God-appointed provision for them. The frank realism here — acknowledging that sexual desire is a real force, not a spiritual defect — is pastoral wisdom of the highest order.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns to a question about divorce, and carefully distinguishes between the Lord’s own command (vv. 10–11, where Jesus’s teaching in the Gospels forbids divorce) and his own apostolic judgment (vv. 12–16, which addresses a situation Jesus did not directly address: the “mixed” marriage between a believer and an unbeliever). The distinction is not between authoritative Scripture and fallible opinion; it is between two levels of apostolic teaching: the direct dominical command and the apostolic application to new situations.

The “Pauline privilege” of vv. 15–16 has been much discussed. If the unbelieving spouse chooses to leave, the believer is not bound — meaning, most naturally, that the believer is not obligated to pursue, beg, or hold on. The reason Paul gives is surprising: “God has called you to peace.” The Christian life is not characterised by endless conflict to maintain a marriage that the unbeliever has already abandoned. Paul is not opening a door to easy divorce but recognising that when an unbelieving spouse has departed, the believing spouse has not failed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s careful distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” vs. “I say, not the Lord”) is a fascinating window into apostolic hermeneutics. It does not mean that vv. 12–16 are less authoritative Scripture — Paul is writing under inspiration. It means that vv. 10–11 apply a dominical teaching directly, while vv. 12–16 extend the principle to a situation Jesus did not address. Both are authoritative; they are transparent about their different relationship to the dominical tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinth had a high divorce rate by ancient standards; the city’s fluid social culture made marriage instability common. The question of what to do in a mixed marriage — especially if the unbeliever wanted out — was live and urgent for many in the community. Now: The “Pauline privilege” continues to be one of the most practically significant and debated passages in NT ethics, applied to situations ranging from desertion to abuse. The governing principle — God has called you to peace — is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Not I, but the Lord” — this is the direct teaching of Jesus on divorce (Matt 5:32; 19:9; Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18). The parenthetical provision — if she does separate, remain unmarried or be reconciled — is not a weakening of the command but a recognition of pastoral reality: if separation has already occurred, the options are reconciliation or continued celibacy. Remarriage to another while the first spouse lives is not presented as a legitimate option here. The symmetry is again notable: both wife separating from husband and husband divorcing wife are addressed equally.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: The “sanctification” of the unbelieving spouse is not their personal salvation but their inclusion in the sphere of the covenant: through the believing spouse, the marriage and its children are brought within the influence of the gospel and the community of God’s people. This is not universalism but a recognition that the believing spouse is not spiritually contaminated by the unbelieving marriage; rather, the direction of holy influence runs from the believer toward the unbeliever. The OT background is the holiness of the covenant household in which even non-Israelites shared in Israel’s blessings.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary: “Not enslaved” — not bound, not obligated to chase the departing spouse. The word dedoulōtai echoes the slavery language of 7:23; the believer who was bought with a price is not to become enslaved to a situation the unbeliever has abandoned. “God has called you to peace” — the vocation of the Christian life is not permanent conflict to hold together what the unbeliever has chosen to dissolve. The question of v. 16 — “how do you know whether you will save your spouse?” — cuts both ways: it may justify staying (you might be the means of their salvation) or it may acknowledge the uncertainty that makes desperate clinging fruitless (you cannot guarantee it).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The governing principle of the chapter appears three times like a refrain: remain in the calling in which you were called (vv. 17, 20, 24). Paul applies it to two examples — circumcision and slavery — to make a point that transcends both: a change of social or physical status is not a spiritual upgrade. The Corinthians appear to have been anxious about their pre-conversion status: the circumcised wondering if they should undo it; the uncircumcised wondering if they should be circumcised; slaves wondering if they should seek freedom. Paul’s counsel is essentially: the gospel does not require a change of external status; it transforms the meaning of the status you are in.

The application to slavery in vv. 21–23 is nuanced. Paul does not command slaves to remain enslaved as a theological principle — “if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity” (v. 21). But he does relativise the difference: the slave who belongs to Christ is the Lord’s freedman; the free person who belongs to Christ is Christ’s slave. The cross inverts and relativises every social category without immediately abolishing them. “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (v. 23) — the one who belongs to Christ in the ultimate sense is not defined by any lesser master.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Relativisation of Social Status by the Gospel

Paul’s refrain — remain as you are — is not social conservatism but theological prioritisation. The gospel relativises every earthly status by subjecting it to a higher identity: in Christ. This does not mean social structures are indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good), but that the gospel’s transformative work operates from the inside out, transforming the meaning of every condition before changing the condition itself. This is the seed from which the ultimate abolition of slavery grew in Christian history: not immediate political revolution but the recognition that the slave is Christ’s freedman, which eventually made the institution of slavery theologically intolerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. The question of whether conversion required a change of social status was real and practically urgent. Paul’s answer guards against two errors: treating social change as spiritually necessary (legalism applied to status), and treating social change as spiritually forbidden (quietism about injustice). Now: The principle “remain as you are” guards against the modern Christian anxiety that effectiveness for God requires a different job, a different social location, a different cultural context. You were placed where you are by Providence; bloom there.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God. Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Assigned” and “called” are both theologically loaded: one’s life circumstances are not accidents but a divine appointment. Circumcision is the test case because it was the hot-button issue of Jewish-Gentile identity in Paul’s churches. His verdict is characteristic: “neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision.” The physical status is theologically irrelevant to one’s standing before God. What matters is “keeping the commandments of God” — which in Paul’s framework means the obedience that flows from faith, the Spirit-empowered life that the commandments describe and that grace alone produces.

verseByVerse.quote: Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.) For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The twin declarations — the slave is Christ’s freedman; the free person is Christ’s slave — relativise the social hierarchy with a completeness that no social revolution could match. Not because the categories disappear but because they are now held under a greater category: belonging to Christ. “Bought with a price” — the same phrase as 6:20 — applied now to the social domain: the person who belongs to Christ by the price of his blood is not available for ultimate ownership by any human institution. “Do not become bondservants of men” — Paul is not forbidding all human authority but warning against the soul-ownership that idolises a master, an employer, a social system, at the expense of the supreme Lordship of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul extends his principles to the specific cases of betrothed virgins and widows, but the thread running through the entire section is the eschatological urgency introduced in v. 26: “in view of the present distress.” Whether this refers to a specific local crisis (famine, persecution) or to the general eschatological pressure of the “last times” is debated; either way, Paul’s counsel is shaped by the sense that the present order is passing (v. 31) and that undivided devotion to the Lord is a genuine good.

The famous “as if not” passage of vv. 29–31 is not a call to emotional detachment or worldly withdrawal but an eschatological relativisation: those who mourn as if not mourning, those who rejoice as if not rejoicing, those who buy as if not possessing. The present is real but not ultimate; the world is passing away. This is not Stoic apathy but the freedom of a person who knows that the ultimate good is secured in Christ and therefore holds all penultimate goods with an open hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eschatological Relativisation and Christian Freedom

Paul’s “as if not” framework is one of the most pastorally liberating texts in the NT for the believer under pressure. It is not an ascetic refusal of the world’s goods but an insistence that no good and no loss in this age has the last word. Marriage, mourning, rejoicing, buying — all are real; none are final. The person who holds them “as if not” is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their ultimate security is not invested in any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress” — the compressed time between the first and second coming, with its attendant pressures. He is not issuing universal commands but pastorally calibrated counsel. Now: The eschatological urgency has not diminished — we are closer to the end than Paul’s Corinth was. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, is not less relevant but more.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I want to spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary: “I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy” — a careful claim: this is apostolic wisdom, not dominical command, but it is authoritative apostolic wisdom offered by one who stands within the Lord’s merciful calling. The “present distress” shapes the practical counsel without making marriage sinful — Paul says three times that marriage is not sin (vv. 28, 36, 38). But worldly troubles attach to marriage in ways that do not attach to singleness, and given the eschatological hour, Paul would spare his people unnecessary encumbrances on their devotion to the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The appointed time has grown very short” — ho kairos synestalmenos estin: the time has been compressed, drawn in, shortened. This is not a prediction about the Parousia’s calendar but a description of the eschatological shape of the present moment: we live in the last act, which has a different quality to everything that precedes it. “As though they had none / were not / had no” — the series is not asceticism but freedom: the hold of earthly things is loosened, not by despising them, but by seeing them in their true proportion. The present form of the world — its social structures, its economic arrangements, its categories of possession and loss — is passing away. Invest in what endures.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife, and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary: The commendation of singleness here is not a devaluation of marriage but an honest acknowledgement of its complexity. The married person has a legitimate second object of devotion — the spouse — and this divides their attention. Paul is not saying this is bad; he is saying it is real. The single person can give the Lord the full bandwidth of their anxiety, concern, and devotion. “Undivided devotion to the Lord” is the one thing Paul is trying to secure — for the married and the single alike, each by the path of their own calling.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry— it is no sin... But if someone stands firm in his resolve, being under no compulsion, and has his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better... A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: “He will do well” / “he will do even better” — the comparison is not between sin and holiness but between two genuinely good options at different altitudes of eschatological freedom. Paul does not command celibacy; he commends it as the higher expression of undivided devotion in the circumstances of the present age. The final verse — “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” — is Paul’s quiet claim that his apostolic judgment, though not a direct dominical command, is Spirit-guided wisdom that carries weight. He is not uncertain; he is epistemically honest about the level of authority he is claiming.

8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
Chapter 8 begins a three-chapter discussion of food offered to idols — one of the most practically complex ethical questions facing first-century Christians in a pagan city. Meat sold in Corinthian markets had typically been offered to a god in the course of slaughter; temple festivals provided occasions for social meals at which the food served had been formally dedicated to a deity; invitations to dinner at a friend’s house might involve food similarly offered. For the Gentile Christian who had been converted from paganism, the question of whether eating such food was spiritually compromising — or whether it was an act of continued idolatry — was urgent and divisive.

Paul’s answer unfolds over three chapters and is more nuanced than either extreme: the “strong” (who know the idol is nothing and eat freely) are correct in their theology but wrong in their love; the “weak” (whose conscience is troubled by the association with idolatry) are incorrect in their theology but are being damaged by the strong’s exercise of freedom. The governing principle that Paul introduces in chapter 8 is the priority of love over knowledge: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (v. 1). Correct theology that ignores its effect on the weaker brother is not mature but immature — the immaturity of knowledge without love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul opens by granting the Corinthians’ theological premise: “we all possess knowledge.” They were right that an idol is nothing, that there is only one God, and that therefore the food offered to an idol has no spiritual contamination. Paul affirms the monotheism of vv. 4–6 wholeheartedly: “there is no God but one,” and the “gods many and lords many” of paganism have no genuine existence. The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is one of the most beautiful christological expansions of the Shema in the NT: the one God of Israel is now confessed as Father from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. The Lordship of Christ is inserted into the centre of Jewish monotheism as its fulfilment.

But — and here is Paul’s first move — knowledge of this kind inflates the one who possesses it. “Knowledge puffs up” (phusioi — the same word used for Corinthian pride throughout the letter). The “strong” in Corinth knew their theology; they also knew they were theologically superior to the weak. And that superiority — the smug confidence that comes from having got it right while others are still confused — is not a sign of spiritual maturity but a sign of having missed the point. “Love builds up” (oikodomei — the building metaphor of ch. 3): the measure of genuine spiritual maturity is not the correctness of your theology but the constructiveness of your love.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Christological Shema and the One Lordship

The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is a watershed in NT christology. Paul takes the foundational monotheistic confession of Israel — “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deut 6:4) — and distributes it between the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. God the Father receives the title “one God” with the phrase “from whom are all things and for whom we exist”; Jesus Christ receives the title “one Lord” with the phrase “through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” Both titles draw on the divine prerogative of creation. This is not bitheism or subordinationism; it is the Shema expanded to include the Son within the identity of the one God of Israel — which is exactly what Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically sophisticated — probably a mix of those with a Jewish background (who knew the idol was nothing) and educated Gentiles who had absorbed the Stoic critique of popular religion. Their knowledge was real. Their pride was realer. Now: The Reformed tradition is not immune to the Corinthian disease of knowledge-pride. The person who has worked through the doctrines of grace and arrived at the Reformation’s conclusions is in real danger of making theological correctness a platform for contempt of those still confused. Paul’s question applies: have you been known by God? (v. 3). That is the only knowledge that ultimately matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes the Corinthian slogan (“all of us possess knowledge”) with a slightly ironic tone — they are proud of what they know. His correction is not that knowledge is bad but that it is insufficient: it inflates the one who has it rather than strengthening the community. “He does not yet know as he ought to know” — the measure of true knowing is not the content of one’s information but the quality of one’s love. The most startling move: “if anyone loves God, he is known by God.” The direction reverses: the primary knowledge is not our knowledge of God but God’s knowledge of us. To be known by God is prior to, and more significant than, knowing things about God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth— as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”— yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary: The theological affirmation is unqualified: the pagan gods have no genuine existence; the one God is the Father who is the source and goal of all things; the one Lord is Jesus Christ through whom all things were made and through whom believers exist. The Shema (Deut 6:4) has been expanded to include Christ within the divine identity — a trinitarian trajectory already present in Paul’s earliest letters. “For us” — this confession is the distinctive self-understanding of the Christian community: we know who the real God is, and that knowledge shapes everything, including our approach to the question of idol food.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The strong have correct theology; but not everyone has this knowledge. Some Corinthians, whose prior devotion had been given to these gods, had not yet made the psychological and spiritual transition to full confidence in the idol’s nonentity. When they eat food offered to idols, they eat it “with consciousness of the idol” — their conscience is troubled, not by correct theological reasoning but by the association with their former religious life. And a conscience troubled in this way, when violated by eating, is a conscience defiled — the person is wounded, not strengthened.

Paul’s principle is clear: the freedom to eat is real, but it is not the supreme value. The weak brother for whom Christ died outweighs the freedom of the strong. “If food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble” (v. 13) — the voluntary limitation of genuine freedom out of love for the weaker brother is Paul’s model and the governing ethic of chapters 8–10. Freedom is real; love is the criterion for when and how to use it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The category of “weak brother” in Paul is not a permanent spiritual classification but a pastoral description of someone whose conscience is not yet formed to the level of theological maturity the gospel makes possible. The strong are not forbidden to exercise their freedom; they are required to consider the effect of their freedom on those still developing. This is not a silencing of the theologically mature but a school in cruciform love: the pattern of Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake became poor” (2 Cor 8:9), is the paradigm for the voluntary limitation of legitimate freedom in love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific situation — food offered to idols in a pagan temple context — is culturally remote for most Western Christians. But the principle is not: the more mature members of any community regularly face the question of how to use their freedom in ways that do not damage those who are less free. Now: The contemporary applications range from alcohol (where an alcoholic is in the room) to entertainment choices (where a recovering addict might be triggered) to musical styles in worship (where real spiritual associations exist for some). The principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Their conscience, being weak, is defiled” — the defilement is not a moral assessment of the action (the food is genuinely harmless) but a description of what happens to the person who acts against their conscience, even in something not intrinsically sinful. The conscience is the moral self-awareness that evaluates actions; when violated, even by something objectively permissible, it leaves a residue of guilt and shame. Paul affirms the strong’s position — food is morally neutral before God — but refuses to let that affirmation override the pastoral concern for the defiled conscience of the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols? And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Destroyed” (apollytai) — the same word used for eternal loss. The weak brother who is led by the strong’s example to eat against his conscience is not merely embarrassed; he is spiritually harmed in a way that threatens his ultimate standing. “The brother for whom Christ died” — the Christological weight of that phrase is the decisive argument. Christ paid the infinite cost of the cross for this person. The strong who treats his freedom as more important than the person for whom Christ died has committed a profound inversion of values. And “sinning against Christ” — because the weak brother is a member of Christ’s body, the wound inflicted on him is felt by Christ himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary: “Never” — categorical, absolute, permanent. Paul does not negotiate or hedge: if the exercise of his genuine freedom is the occasion of a brother’s spiritual harm, he will permanently forego it. This is the cruciform logic applied to daily life: the willingness to absorb genuine loss — the loss of a legitimate freedom — for the sake of a sibling. Keller: “Paul is not saying ‘I’ll try to be careful.’ He is saying: I would rather be hungry for the rest of my life than be the occasion of my brother’s stumbling. That is what love that has been shaped by the cross looks like.”

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is Paul’s longest and most personal argument for the principle he stated in chapter 8: voluntary limitation of genuine freedom out of love for others. He uses himself as the exhibit. He has apostolic rights — the right to be supported financially by the churches he serves, the right to travel with a believing wife, the right to be exempt from manual labour. These rights are real; Paul defends them at length from Scripture, common sense, and analogy. And then he announces that he has used none of them. He preaches the gospel free of charge, works with his own hands, and makes himself a slave to everyone in order to win as many as possible.

The chapter is therefore both the longest example in the letter of the principle of self-limitation in love and a defence of Paul’s ministry against those at Corinth who questioned his apostleship on the grounds that he did not accept financial support. The two are connected: the very thing they criticise him for — refusing payment — is the thing that demonstrates the principle he is asking them to follow. He is not asking them to do something he is unwilling to do himself. The chapter ends with the image of the athlete: the runner who submits to severe self-discipline in order to win the race. The Christian life is not passive; it requires the kind of focused, costly self-discipline that any serious competitor knows.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul establishes his apostolic credentials and defends his rights with a series of arguments: analogy (soldiers, farmers, shepherds all receive the fruit of their work), Scripture (the ox treading grain must not be muzzled — Deut 25:4), common sense (the one who ploughs should plough in hope), and the Lord’s own command (those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel, v. 14). By the time he has finished, the right of the apostle to financial support is as well-established as any right in the letter.

The purpose of this lengthy defence is not to claim the right but to set up its voluntary surrender. Paul builds the case meticulously so that when he says “I have made no use of any of these rights” (v. 15), the reader understands what has been surrendered. The magnitude of the renunciation corresponds to the length of the defence. This is not Paul being merely practical (I prefer to earn my own income); it is a deliberately chosen posture of love that refuses to let anything — even a legitimate financial right — become an obstacle to the gospel.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Right of Ministers to Financial Support

Paul’s argument from Deuteronomy 25:4 (“Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain”) follows a characteristic pattern in his hermeneutics: the OT command for the benefit of animals carries an “how much more” application to human ministers of the gospel. The principle that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7, quoted by Paul in 1 Tim 5:18) is embedded in the creation order and confirmed by the Lord’s own command. The Reformed tradition has always insisted on adequate financial support for ordained ministry as a matter of justice, not charity — grounded precisely in passages like this.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The travelling sophist in Corinth charged fees for his teaching; the apostle who did not was, paradoxically, suspected of being less legitimate — not worth paying. Paul’s refusal to accept payment actually undermined his status in the eyes of some Corinthians, which is why he defends the right even while refusing to exercise it. Now: The principle cuts in two directions: congregations should support their ministers generously; ministers should never let financial considerations drive their preaching agenda. The apostle who can preach without anxiety about whether his congregation will like what they hear is the freest preacher in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. This is my defense to those who would examine me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four rapid questions, each asserting a fundamental truth. Freedom — he is a free person, not obligated to anyone. Apostleship — he carries the commission of the risen Christ. Seeing the Lord — the basis of his apostolic claim is the Damascus road appearance, as real and defining as the appearances to the Twelve. And the Corinthians themselves — “the seal of my apostleship.” If any evidence were needed that Paul’s ministry was authentic, the very existence of the Corinthian church — converted through his preaching — provides it. The people questioning his credentials were themselves his credentials.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
